```{r setup}
library(blockr.core)
```

A blockr app runs in two places.
The browser holds the board, and R evaluates its blocks.
Both sides write log lines.
Both can also record spans, which time what each side does.
By default, R writes its log lines to standard output and standard error, and the browser writes its own to the browser's console.
Neither side records spans.

[OpenTelemetry](https://opentelemetry.io/) gives log records and spans a common format.
Its collector is a program that receives them and passes them on to wherever a deployment keeps them.
This guide shows how a deployment sends the log records and spans of both sides to one collector, whichever host runs the app.
No record leaves R or the page until the deployment sets where it goes.

## What each side sends

R sends a log record for each line that core or a package writes through `write_log()`, at the level that the blockr option `log_level` sets or above.
That includes every condition that R sends the browser, such as the error of a block.
The record of a block's condition names the block and its revision.
R also records a span of each evaluation, output and request that the browser asks for.
Inside the span of an evaluation, it records a span of each phase of the evaluation.

The browser sends a log record for each line that the code on the page writes, such as every failure that core catches, with its stack.
It records a span of each command, such as an edit of a block, and of each evaluation, output and request that it sends to R.
It also records a span of the page's start and of each opening of a board.

Each request that the browser sends carries the context of the browser's span of the request.
So R's span of the request is a child of the browser's span, in the same trace.
The span of an evaluation links to the span of the command that changed the block.
Both sides name the session in every record and span by `session.id`, which holds Shiny's token of the session.
So a collector joins the records of one session from both sides.

Spans hold IDs and revisions, never a block's state or data.
Log records hold messages, such as the message of a block's error, which may quote the block's data.
So the collector, and wherever it passes the records on, needs the care that R's logs need.

## One collector for both sides

A deployment runs one [OpenTelemetry collector](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/collector/) for both sides.
R sends its records to the collector from the server, and the browser of every user sends its own from the page.
So the collector must be reachable from R, and from the browser of every user.

Both sides send over OTLP/HTTP, OpenTelemetry's protocol over HTTP.
This configuration of the collector receives log records and spans on the default port of OTLP/HTTP, 4318.
It listens on `localhost` alone, where R and a proxy on the same server reach it.
It passes both on to a backend at `https://otlp.example.com`:

```yaml
receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      http:
        endpoint: localhost:4318

exporters:
  otlphttp:
    endpoint: https://otlp.example.com

service:
  pipelines:
    traces:
      receivers: [otlp]
      exporters: [otlphttp]
    logs:
      receivers: [otlp]
      exporters: [otlphttp]
```

The collector's [configuration](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/collector/configuration/) lists its other receivers and exporters.

## R

R exports through the package [otelsdk](https://otelsdk.r-lib.org/), which OpenTelemetry's environment variables set up.
These variables have R send its spans and log records to the collector above, which runs on the same server.
They also name the app's service, and keep Shiny's own spans to sessions:

```sh
OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER=otlp
OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER=otlp
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:4318
OTEL_SERVICE_NAME=iris-review
SHINY_OTEL_COLLECT=session
```

R sends its spans to the path `v1/traces` below the endpoint, and its log records to `v1/logs`.
The [environment variables of otelsdk](https://otelsdk.r-lib.org/reference/environmentvariables.html) include others, such as those for headers and certificates.
The package otelsdk must be installed where the app runs, since blockr.core suggests it but does not import it.

A deployment uses `otlp` as the exporter.
That exporter sends from a thread of its own.
The console and file exporters of otelsdk write each record on R's thread, and an evaluation waits while they write.

Shiny records spans of its own wherever R exports spans.
By default, Shiny records a trace for each message that the browser sends.
Such a trace shows little more than the observer that takes the message.
The value `session` of `SHINY_OTEL_COLLECT` keeps Shiny's spans to the start and the end of each session, as [Shiny's options](https://shiny.posit.co/r/reference/shiny/latest/shinyoptions.html) describe.

Where the blockr option `logger` is not set, R writes its log lines through OpenTelemetry once `OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER` sets up an exporter, and to the console otherwise.
The blockr option `log_level` sets the lowest level that each side writes.
It is info unless set.
OpenTelemetry's own level, `OTEL_LOG_LEVEL`, drops none of core's records.
Where `logger` is `"otel"`, each side stops where it has nowhere to send, rather than writing to the console.
The help of `write_log()` gives the details.

## The browser

The browser sends its log records and spans to the collector whose URL the blockr option `otel_client_endpoint` gives.
The blockr option `otel_client_service_name` names the page's service in its records, as `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` names R's.
It is `blockr` where it is not set.
A deployment sets both as environment variables:

```sh
BLOCKR_OTEL_CLIENT_ENDPOINT=/otlp/
BLOCKR_OTEL_CLIENT_SERVICE_NAME=iris-review-browser
```

Like every blockr option, each can also be set as an R option, as in an app script:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
options(blockr.otel_client_endpoint = "/otlp/")
```

The browser sends its spans to the path `v1/traces` below the URL, and its log records to `v1/logs`.
A relative URL is read against the page.
So `/otlp/` names the path `/otlp/` on the page's own host, whatever the path of the app on that host.

The browser sends its records in batches.
It also sends what it holds as the page is hidden, as when the user switches to another tab or closes the page.
Where `otel_client_endpoint` is not set, the browser writes its log lines to its console, records no spans and loads none of OpenTelemetry's SDK.

## Under the app's host name

Where a proxy sits in front of the app, it can route a path of the app's host name, here `/otlp/`, to the collector.
With NGINX, a `location` block for the path goes beside the block that routes the rest to the app:

```nginx
location /otlp/ {
  proxy_pass http://localhost:4318/;
}
```

The trailing slash of `proxy_pass` drops `/otlp` from the path.
So a record that the browser sends to `/otlp/v1/logs` reaches the collector at `/v1/logs`.
With `/otlp/` as `BLOCKR_OTEL_CLIENT_ENDPOINT`, the page sends its records to its own origin, so it needs no CORS.

On Posit Connect, for example, the administrator adds the route to the proxy in front of Connect ([Running with a proxy](https://docs.posit.co/connect/admin/proxy/)).
The publisher sets the environment variables of the sections above in the settings of the content ([Environment variables](https://docs.posit.co/connect/user/content-settings/#environment-variables)).
Connect can send its own telemetry to the same collector ([OpenTelemetry](https://docs.posit.co/connect/admin/opentelemetry/)).

## At another origin

A collector at another origin than the page must allow the page's requests through CORS.
So it lists the page's origin in the `cors.allowed_origins` of its OTLP/HTTP receiver, as its [HTTP settings](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector/blob/main/config/confighttp/README.md#server-configuration) describe:

```yaml
receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      http:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318
        cors:
          allowed_origins:
            - https://apps.example.com
```

The app then names the collector by its full URL, as in `BLOCKR_OTEL_CLIENT_ENDPOINT=https://otel.example.com/`.
The list never holds `*`.
A browser accepts it, and the pages of any site could then send records to the collector from the browsers of their visitors.

A hosted backend usually takes records only with a key, but the browser sends no header of its own.
So the browser sends its records to the deployment's own collector.
That collector passes them on to the backend, with the key in the settings of its exporter.
